content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Expert Committee on Biological Standardization (ECBS) will establish a process for the production and validation of reference materials in 2019. Between 2020 and 2022, the ECBS will adopt technical specifications for individual venom and antivenom reference standards. The production of reference standards for WHO antivenom prequalification will commence in 2023–2024. Following this, a WHO antivenom prequalification program will be established. Prequalification ensures that national regulatory agencies and other organizations can provide high-quality medicines to those in need. It also instills confidence in purchasers, donors, and users that the medicines are safe, effective, and manufactured to high standards. Some organizations only support the procurement of prequalified medicines. The introduction of prequalified antivenoms will significantly rehabilitate the antivenom market and ensure its sustainability. Manufacturers will gain access to antivenom prequalification in 2023–2024, and products meeting the required standards will be available for procurement. The demand for prequalified antivenoms will stimulate the market, increasing supply, affordability, and sustainability of well-designed, safe, and effective antivenoms. Prequalification will also facilitate the inclusion of antivenom products in medicine financing programs and encourage investment in innovative research for new therapeutics. A lack of investment limits manufacturers' ability to improve production, conduct research and development, and finance essential infrastructure improvements. Modest investments in strengthening manufacturing, developing, and validating new products are critical to overcoming the current supply crisis. Investment in delivering new treatments to the market will immediately reduce mortality, morbidity, and disability. This strategy will stimulate investment for the rapid delivery of new treatments for snakebite envenoming in regions currently lacking effective products. If manufacturers can access capital to modernize production infrastructure, introduce new technologies, and invest in research, new products will be introduced in sufficient quantities to address chronic shortages, with measurable improvements in health outcomes. However, most manufacturers lack resources for innovative research, and academic research on antivenoms often fails to align with industry needs. Partnerships and collaborations between academia and industry could strengthen, innovate, and expand production, quality control, preclinical and clinical testing, and pharmacovigilance of antivenoms and other treatments, leading to rapid improvements in access to safe and effective antivenoms. The strategy will support innovative and collaborative research between industry and academia. Research and development into new products, processes, and other areas will accelerate with support from research funding agencies. New therapeutic candidates will be identified to ensure drug development pipelines deliver next-generation treatments by 2030. Health workers often receive little to no training in diagnosing and treating snakebite envenoming, with limited opportunities for in-service professional development. Training packages should be integrated into health worker curricula at all levels to improve the management of snakebite envenoming. Locally relevant training materials will be prepared to enhance health workers' knowledge and practical clinical competence. Improved management of snakebite envenoming and overall clinical practice will benefit all patients. Regular in-service training in clinical skills for snakebite envenoming management is essential, particularly for rural health workers who often lack such opportunities. Training in skills relevant to snakebite envenoming improves overall clinical practice. Workforce training measures adopted by Member States would directly improve and standardize treatment and recovery. Snakebite envenoming is poorly covered in most tertiary and vocational training curricula for health professionals, leaving graduates ill-equipped to manage such cases. Integrating clinical toxinology into training programs will enhance patient care and treatment at all levels. Teaching health workers to properly treat snakebites provides them with fundamental cross-cutting clinical skills. Education on snakebite prevention and treatment in medical, nursing, and other health professional curricula will better prepare health workers to manage snakebite envenoming confidently. Efforts to improve training would benefit from clinical toxinology becoming a recognized medical specialty coordinated by a professional college or association. Few resources are available to help health professionals improve the care and treatment of snakebite envenoming. The availability of appropriate guidelines, resources, and tools will improve clinical practice. Guidelines and learning tools will be developed to standardize prevention, clinical diagnosis, treatment, recovery, and rehabilitation of snakebite patients. Standardized clinical criteria for envenoming syndromes will be defined in consensus documents with clear clinical endpoints for treatment effectiveness. Health workers will be better equipped to diagnose snakebite envenoming objectively and identify specific clinical syndromes, improving case management. Standardized tools will support decision-making and improve treatment outcomes, enabling more reliable data analysis and comparison. Current point-of-care diagnostic tests for snakebite envenoming could be made more accurate and reliable, reducing treatment delays and improving patient outcomes. A framework will be developed for delivering innovative new point-of-care diagnostic tools. Post-acute care and services for disability support and rehabilitation have been neglected. Critical pathways should include these elements of treatment and recovery. Adoption of such measures by Member States will directly improve and standardize treatment and recovery, increasing access to care and support during recovery. Awareness will be raised about the rehabilitation needs of snakebite victims, and strategies will be developed to increase access to rehabilitation services to accelerate recovery. Rehabilitation care providers will deliver necessary services to hasten recovery and enable snakebite envenoming patients with disabilities to return to productive lives. Current medical management focuses primarily on the acute phase, with post-discharge care often excluded from health professional training. The importance of after-care should be included in management protocols to ensure all snakebite patients are followed up. Follow-up care will increase participation in recovery and rehabilitation, reducing morbidity and disability. Comprehensive snakebite envenoming management protocols, medical and health worker training curricula, guidelines, and tools will be prepared. Strengthening health systems is fundamental to improving snakebite envenoming treatment. Rural primary health services, district secondary, sub-national, and national tertiary health services should be strengthened in line with Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3) and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) 2030. Targeted investment will be sought to build peripheral infrastructure and increase access to effective healthcare, including transport, communications, and support services, to improve healthcare access for all citizens. Many regulatory agencies, drug control laboratories, and health authorities lack the technical capacity to regulate and control the safety, effectiveness, and quality of antivenoms marketed in their countries. Improving their capacity to undertake normative, regulatory, and laboratory activities will enhance access to safe, effective, quality-assured antivenoms and other medicines. Innovative, validated systems for the procurement, distribution, and surveillance of antivenoms are essential to overcome logistical, infrastructure, and communication challenges in remote rural communities. Pragmatic investment in emerging technologies, such as low-cost portable cold chains, delivery systems, and mobile surveillance tools, should be encouraged. Research will be conducted to improve the implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of innovative interventions to enhance distribution systems and post-marketing surveillance of antivenom safety and effectiveness in health facilities and communities. New approaches will be introduced for the procurement, distribution, and surveillance of antivenoms. Stronger, more effective supply chains and surveillance systems will ensure timely and reliable access to antivenoms and other essential medical products.
